implementation_notes: Express's middleware chain is the checkpoint: a guard mounted on the router (api.use(passport.authenticate('jwt', { session: false }))) protects every route declared after it, and Passport strategies are the delegated mechanism. TypeScript adds the principal to the request type through declaration merging (declare global namespace Express { interface Request { user?: Principal } }), so handlers read req.user with types; Fastify's equivalent is a preHandler hook. Prefer this when the stack is Express/Fastify; the enforcement stays one mounted guard, not a per-handler check.
pitfalls: Declaration merging types req.user but does not guarantee it exists: a route mounted before the guard still compiles and runs unauthenticated.
The non-null assertion is only honest after the guard has run; prefer a typed AuthenticatedRequest or an explicit assert helper when handlers are reused outside the guarded router.

variants.name: NestJS guard (CanActivate) with @UseGuards
variants.implementation_notes: NestJS makes the checkpoint a class guard: AuthGuard implements CanActivate, reads the request from ExecutionContext, delegates verification to an injected strategy or service, and either throws UnauthorizedException (the challenge) or returns false. Guards bind per controller or handler with @UseGuards, or globally through the APP_GUARD provider so the default is deny; a custom @Public() decorator plus Reflector metadata marks the explicit exceptions. The mechanism is a provider injected into the guard, so it stays swappable exactly as the pattern requires.
pitfalls: Register the guard through the APP_GUARD provider, not app.useGlobalGuards(new AuthGuard(...)): instances created outside the container lose dependency injection for the verifier and the Reflector.
Returning false from a guard yields 403 Forbidden; throw UnauthorizedException instead when the correct challenge is 401 - the two statuses describe different failures.
